Yen: the dollar stalls just below 160 yen, the line where Tokyo and Washington intervened together this summer

On Tuesday, November 24, the dollar was worth about 158.95 yen in Asia, after nearly touching 160 yen. Currency traders fear a new intervention by Tokyo, which spent a record 15.4 trillion yen last summer, partly alongside Washington. The Bank of Japan could raise rates on December 18 [1][3][11].
On Tuesday morning in Asia, the dollar slipped toward 158.95 yen: fear of an intervention by the Japanese authorities is supporting the Japanese currency [1].

Currency traders see the threshold of 160 yen to the dollar as a possible trigger for a new intervention, even though the figure is in no way official [1][14]. On Monday, the yen had initially weakened, as the rally on Wall Street pushed investors toward riskier assets [2].
Finance Minister Satsuki Katayama warned against “one-sided” currency moves, as the dollar spent much of November just below 160 yen [3].
Futures markets put the chance of a Bank of Japan rate hike on December 18 at about 85% [3]. A majority of economists polled by Reuters expect it to reach 1.5%, up from 1.25% today [4].
Within the Bank of Japan, however, Toichiro Asada is calling for caution: raising rates too quickly could break the lasting inflation the country took years to achieve [5].
On the other side, US inflation remains strong and markets are betting on Fed rate hikes, which keeps the interest rate gap in the dollar's favor [6][1].
Next test: the PCE price index, the Fed's preferred inflation gauge, released Wednesday in the United States [1].

Key takeaway: the yen is weakening because money earns far more in the United States than in Japan. Investors borrow in yen, at 1.25% [4], to invest in dollars at higher rates. As long as this gap stays wide, the yen struggles to recover [1].
Tokyo has two weapons. The first is intervention: selling dollars from its reserves to buy yen. It has already been used three times in four years, without reversing the trend [8][9][11].

The second is a Bank of Japan rate hike, which would narrow the gap with the United States. With core inflation at 2.2% in October [1], a hike in December is becoming likely [3]. But the central bank is hesitant to slow a fragile economy too much [5].
The decision also depends on Washington: strong US inflation on Wednesday would push the dollar toward 160 yen and bring an intervention closer [1].

A weak yen makes Japan cheaper for a French tourist: your hotel and restaurant budget there goes further. Conversely, Japanese cars and electronics become more competitive against European products. If an intervention happens, the yen can jump several percent within a few hours.

How it works: a currency market intervention

When the yen falls too fast, Japan's Ministry of Finance can order the Bank of Japan to sell dollars, taken from the country's reserves, and buy yen. This sudden demand pushes the yen back up. In September 2022, such an operation lifted the yen by as much as 2.6% within a few hours [7]. But the effect is often temporary: intervention does not change the interest rate gap between Japan and the United States, which pushes the yen down [15]. That is why Tokyo tries to surprise markets, and why joint action with Washington, as on July 31, 2026 [12][13], carries more weight: it shows that both countries want the same thing.
Precedents: Tokyo comes to the yen's rescue
September 22, 2022
The yen falls to 145.90 to the dollar, its lowest since 1998. Tokyo buys yen for the first time since 1998 [7] and spends 2.84 trillion yen ($19.7 billion) in September [8].
The yen rebounds at first, but the interest rate gap with the United States remains intact [15].
April-May 2024

After a 34-year low of 160.245 yen to the dollar, Japan spends 9.79 trillion yen ($62 billion) between late April and late May, a record at the time [9], without managing to reverse the yen's decline for good [10].
This is where the 160-yen line watched by markets comes from.
July 30-August 2026

Tokyo buys a record 15.4 trillion yen, including 7.98 trillion on July 30 alone [11]. On July 31, the US Treasury buys 79.4 billion yen (about $497 million): a joint action, the first since 1998 [12][13].
Even with Washington's support, the dollar returned to around 159-160 yen within four months [1][11].

Permian Basin: Texas Pacific Land buys EagleRock for $3 billion paid in stock, the target jumps, the buyer falls

On Monday, November 23, Texas Pacific Land, a major owner of oil land in Texas, announced the acquisition of Houston-based EagleRock Land [2] for about $3 billion, paid entirely in stock. EagleRock shares jumped 10 to 15%; the buyer's shares fell nearly 3% [1][3][5].
EagleRock shareholders will receive 0.0831 share of the new group for each share held, or about $23.56 per share based on Texas Pacific Land's five-day average price as of November 20 [1][6].
After the deal, Texas Pacific Land shareholders will own about 86% of the group, and EagleRock shareholders 14% [1].
The acquisition adds about 59,000 acres of fee-simple land in the Delaware Basin, in New Mexico, and increases acreage in the Midland Basin by nearly 40% [1][3].
It also brings processing capacity of about 220,000 barrels per day of “produced water,” the salt water that comes up with the oil [1][3].
Management expects about $45 million a year in gains from the combination [1]. Both boards of directors approved the agreement unanimously [7].
EagleRock shares jumped 10.8% according to GuruFocus, and up to 15% according to Seeking Alpha [4][3]. Texas Pacific Land fell nearly 3% late in the session, in a sharply rising market [5].
Texas Pacific Land's board also raised its share buyback program to $500 million in total [5].

Key takeaway: in US shale oil, those who earn most consistently are not always the drillers, but the landowners. They lease their land, sell access and manage water, whoever the driller is: it is this “land and water portfolio” that TPL is expanding [3].

Water has become a key issue: every barrel extracted from the Permian Basin comes up with large quantities of salt water that must be transported and treated. With 220,000 additional barrels per day of capacity [1], Texas Pacific Land strengthens a business that is less dependent on the price of crude.
The timing is unusual: Brent has fallen near its lowest level in three months, below $89 [8]. Paying in stock rather than cash lets the buyer keep its cash and shares the risk with the sellers [1].
The drop in the buyer's share price [5] shows that its shareholders are worried about dilution: their shares will represent 86% of the new group, instead of 100% [1].

This deal does not affect you directly, but it shows how US oil is reorganizing: players are consolidating through acquisitions. If you have a US equity fund, these “land and royalty” companies are sometimes included: their revenue remains tied to the price of a barrel.

How it works: an acquisition paid in stock

In an “all-stock” acquisition, the buyer pays no cash: it hands over its own shares. An exchange ratio is set, here 0.0831 share of the new group for one EagleRock share [1]. The value received by the seller therefore changes every day with the buyer's share price. Announced at about $23.56 per share based on the average price as of November 20 [1], it falls if Texas Pacific Land shares drop, as they did on Monday [5]. Advantage for the buyer: it keeps its cash. Drawback: its shareholders are diluted, here to 86% of the new group [1]. It is the same type of deal as CrowdStrike's acquisition of Zscaler, announced the same day [9].
Precedents: stock and cash acquisitions
October 2017
The roughly $20 billion “merger of equals” between Swiss company Clariant and US company Huntsman is abandoned on October 27, after activist funds bought more than 20% of Clariant to oppose it [11].
An all-stock deal must win over shareholders on both sides: here, the EagleRock vote is still to come [1].
November 17, 2026
Finland's Iceye offers €2.05 billion in cash, €41 per share, for Italy's Avio, about 20% above the share price; Avio shares gain more than 13% [10].
With cash, the seller knows the exact price; with stock, it depends on the buyer's share price.
November 23, 2026
The same day, CrowdStrike announces the acquisition of Zscaler for about $43.9 billion, entirely in stock, at a premium of about 34% [9].
In the middle of a stock market correction, buyers prefer to pay in stock rather than drain their cash.

Jamaican opposition leader Mark Golding has been demanding since November 23 that Prime Minister Andrew Holness explain himself before Parliament. An audit revealed that the disaster agency (ODPEM) used about 33 million Jamaican dollars in donations intended for Hurricane Melissa victims for other purposes [1][2][3].

According to the Auditor General's report, this money, taken from a donation account reserved for roof repairs and temporary housing, was used to pay customs clearance fees on goods for third parties [3][4].
